primitives.name: Bivariate Conditional Poisson Regression
primitives.verbatim_quote: In this paper, we develop a Bayesian bivariate Conditional Poisson (BCP) regression model to explicitly capture the dependence between home and away goal counts, addressing a core limitation of traditional football scoring models that assume independence or only allow for positive correlation.
primitives.assumptions: Poisson distributed goal counts, log-linear covariate relationships, conditional independence given latent factors

reasoning_traces.think:
The BCP model extends the classic Dixon-Coles framework by jointly modeling home and away goals as conditionally Poisson-distributed random variables, allowing for asymmetric dependence structures. This addresses the common failure mode of assuming independence, which inflates the probability of extreme scores and produces poorly calibrated confidence intervals for match outcomes. By incorporating stadium attendance and fouls as covariates, the model captures game-theoretic feedback loops: higher attendance may increase home-team aggression but also defensive pressure, creating a negative carryover effect on away-team scoring opportunities. The negative correlation we estimate suggests that when one team scores more than expected, the opposing team tends to score less, likely due to shifts in possession, tempo, and risk-taking. This结构性relationship is crucial for GSI because it directly impacts over/under betting lines and halftime predictions; for GSE, it informs state-transition matrices used in sequential decision-making algorithms. The Bayesian treatment via HMC provides full posterior distributions, avoiding frequentist point estimates that obscure tail uncertainty.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The BCP model builds on the bivariate Poisson work of Karlis and Ntzoufras (2003) and the conditional specification of Joe and Li (2010). It differs from earlier approaches by using a Cholesky decomposition of the precision matrix, ensuring positive definiteness of the covariance structure. The use of log-linear intensity functions traces back to the seminal work of Cox (1972) on proportional hazards models. The incorporation of covariates follows the generalized linear modeling framework of McCullagh and Nelder (1989).
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Opposing teams adjust their strategies based on live scorelines and crowd pressure. When the home team scores early, the away team may adopt a more defensive posture, reducing its own scoring chances. Conversely, if the away team scores, the home team might push forward more aggressively, increasing its fouls and potentially leading to fewer high-quality scoring opportunities. The model captures these dynamic adjustments through the negative correlation parameter, which reflects the average behavioral response across all matches.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: To avoid anti-collinearity issues, we must ensure that attendance and fouls are not perfectly collinear, as this would lead to identification problems. Additionally, we impose a leakage veto by conditioning on observed covariates rather than unobserved team quality, preventing spurious correlations driven by omitted variable bias.
